nameStory: The Humphrey Wentletrap gets its first name from someone named Humphrey who likely first described or studied this species. The word 'wentletrap' comes from Dutch meaning 'spiral staircase,' perfectly describing the beautiful ribbed, spiraling shell that looks like a tiny architectural wonder from the sea.
description: The Humphrey Wentletrap is a small marine snail with an elegant, tower-like shell that spirals upward like a miniature staircase. This sea snail is actually a predator or parasite that feeds on sea anemones and other soft-bodied marine creatures. Its shell is typically white to cream-colored with distinct raised ribs running across each whorl, creating the characteristic 'staircase' appearance. These delicate shells are rarely found intact on New England beaches, making any discovery a special treat.

idTips.label: Spiral Shell Structure
idTips.description: Look for a tall, pointed shell that spirals upward in a cone shape with distinct ridged 'steps' or ribs crossing each whorl horizontally, feeling smooth between the raised ribs when you run your finger along it

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: Typically white, cream, or pale yellow with a glossy, almost porcelain-like finish that feels smooth and cool to the touch

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Small shells usually less than an inch tall, easily fitting in the palm of your hand and light as a feather when picked up

idTips.label: Rib Pattern
idTips.description: Distinct raised ridges run horizontally across the shell whorls, creating a ladder-like pattern that you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Shell Opening
idTips.description: Round to oval opening at the base with smooth edges, often with the shell feeling hollow and delicate when held

habitat: Found in deeper waters off the New England coast, typically living on sandy or muddy bottoms where sea anemones are present. Empty shells occasionally wash up on sandy beaches, especially after storms, but finding one is quite rare in New England waters.

seasonality.spring: Storm-tossed shells may wash ashore on beaches after winter storms subside. Look among other shell debris in wrack lines.
seasonality.summer: Peak beachcombing season when any shells that do appear are most likely to be found by active searchers along the tide line.
seasonality.fall: Fall storms may bring shells from deeper waters to shore. Check beaches after nor'easters and strong coastal storms.
seasonality.winter: Harsh winter storms can occasionally drive shells ashore, but cold weather makes beachcombing less pleasant and productive.

funFact: Wentletrap snails can actually detach their own foot (the part they use to crawl) as a defense mechanism when attacked by predators, leaving the foot behind while they escape - and then they regrow it completely!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small spiral shells, but the distinctive horizontal ribs crossing each whorl like stair steps are unique to wentletraps. Remember: if it looks like a tiny spiral staircase, it's probably a wentletrap.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their delicate appearance, these snails are actually fierce predators that drill holes in sea anemones and coral polyps to feed. The beautiful shells have been prized by collectors for centuries, once being worth their weight in gold in some parts of the world.
compareHints: The Humphrey Wentletrap is extremely similar to Champion's Wentletrap, the only other species in its genus found in New England waters. The differences between these two species are so subtle that they typically require expert examination and sometimes microscopic details to distinguish reliably. Both share the same distinctive spiral staircase shell structure with horizontal ribs.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Champion's Wentletrap differs from its close relative Humphrey's Wentletrap primarily in the spacing and prominence of its spiral ridges – Champion's has more numerous, finer ridges that are closer together, creating a more delicate overall appearance.
